# CLI gameplay

Build a complete local two-player tic-tac-toe game from the existing Go seed.
Two people share one terminal. Use only the Go standard library, with rules in
internal/game and command input/output in cmd/tictactoe.

Run with go run ./cmd/tictactoe or build the tictactoe executable. Show a 3x3 ASCII
board with empty cells numbered 1 through 9. X starts; alternate X and O after
each valid move. Read one numbered position per line from standard input.
Trim surrounding whitespace. Explain invalid text, out-of-range positions and
occupied cells, then let the same player try again without changing the board.

Detect all eight winning lines and a draw when the board fills without a winner.
Print the final board and a clear result, then exit successfully. End-of-input
must exit cleanly without hanging or reporting a winner. Keep the seed's --help
and -h behavior. The first version ends after one game; replay is out of scope.

Keep the existing module and package layout. Exclude networking, persistence,
accounts, AI opponents, colors and terminal frameworks. Use deterministic tests
for moves, invalid input, turn preservation, every winning line, draws and EOF.
Exercise the real command boundary as well as the game rules. Validation is
go test ./...; demonstrate a complete X win and a draw using scripted input.

Keep the implementation plan small and cohesive: one slice covering the rules,
CLI integration and regression tests. Preserve working seed behavior and commit
completed task changes for review and integration.

## Settled behavior and implementation choices

These decisions were already answered in an earlier authoring exercise. Treat them as requirements. Remaining ordinary Go implementation choices are delegated to the worker; do not add features.

### Decision 1

Invalid input. Enter a number from 1 to 9.
Position out of range. Enter a number from 1 to 9.
That position is occupied. Choose an empty cell.

Print the appropriate line to stdout and keep the current player and board unchanged.

### Decision 2

Use exactly these stdout lines after printing the final board:
Player X wins!
Player O wins!
It's a draw!

Exit with status 0 after a completed game. On EOF before completion, print Game ended. and exit 0 without declaring a winner or draw. The move prompts are Player X, choose a position (1-9): and Player O, choose a position (1-9):. Preserve the existing --help/-h usage behavior. Keep the board simple: three ASCII rows, X/O for occupied cells, 1-9 for empty cells, vertical bars and horizontal separators.

### Decision 3

Use these five lines for the empty board (each cell row has one leading and trailing space):
 1 | 2 | 3 
---+---+---
 4 | 5 | 6 
---+---+---
 7 | 8 | 9 

Cell values are replaced by X or O after a valid move; all spacing and separators stay the same. Print the board initially, after each valid move and once as the final board before the result. Do not redraw after invalid input. Print each move prompt on its own line, so scripted stdin also yields readable stdout. A single blank line between boards and prompts is sufficient; no banner or terminal-clearing escape sequences are required.

### Decision 4

Print only Game ended. on EOF before completion. The board was already printed initially or after the last valid move, so do not redraw it for EOF. Exit with status 0 and do not report a winner or draw.

### Decision 5

Reject malformed input; never accept a valid digit and ignore trailing characters. Trim surrounding whitespace and parse the entire line as a decimal integer, using strconv.Atoi semantics. Inputs such as 3x, 3 4 and 3.0 print Invalid input. Enter a number from 1 to 9. Integers such as 0, -1 and 10 print Position out of range. Enter a number from 1 to 9. Both rejections preserve the board and current player. Only a parsed position from 1 through 9 can place a mark.

### Decision 6

Exactly one blank line between every printed board and the following move prompt, including the initial prompt. Use one blank line before the final result too. An invalid-input message is followed by a newline and the same player's prompt, without redrawing the board.

### Decision 7

Yes. All normal gameplay output, validation messages, EOF handling, help and final results go to stdout. Keep stderr empty in those cases. Reserve stderr and a nonzero exit status for genuine input/output failures, not an invalid move or ordinary EOF.

### Decision 8

No trailing space. Print each move prompt on its own line, ending immediately after the colon with a newline; user input is on the following line. Preserve the exact errors, results, board and blank-line rules already specified. All other cosmetic details are explicitly delegated to the implementation using conventional CLI defaults. They do not require additional product decisions or extra features. Behavioral correctness and deterministic tests are the acceptance boundary.

### Decision 9

Build one temporary tictactoe binary once for the command-boundary test group, then execute it for each deterministic input case. Use temporary directories and preserve the existing go.mod version. Do not run go run separately for each case or add external test dependencies. Keep package-level game-rule tests separate, and make go test ./... the single validation command. All other implementation choices are delegated to ordinary Go conventions; the functional scope is complete.

### Decision 10

Yes. Build the test binary once with a bounded build deadline, then run each integration case with a 5-second context timeout and fail if it expires. Use t.TempDir for cleanup. This is ordinary test engineering, not an additional product requirement. All remaining implementation and test-engineering choices are explicitly delegated to chr. The scope is a small Go-standard-library, two-human tic-tac-toe CLI with no extra features. Its rules, exact stdout messages, board rendering, help behavior, invalid-move behavior, EOF handling, validation command and test strategy are all defined in the saved Dump and answers. A useful specification can now be written; no further product decisions are required.
